newsitem.title: FRANCE: French police nip new immigrants protest in bud.
newsitem.headline: French police nip new immigrants protest in bud.

text.p: French police nipped a protest by illegal Asian immigrants in the bud on Sunday, preventing them from opening a new front to demonstrate against the conservative government's hardline immigration policies.

About 500 riot police swooped on Saint-Jean Baptiste Roman Catholic church in Paris at dawn to evict 400 Asian immigrants who occupied it on Saturday at the same time as a march against a bill to stiffen a crackdown on illegal immigration.

The immigrant families, most of them Chinese, claimed hardened legislation had deprived them of residence rights. They had brought mattresses to settle in for a long stay, but left peacefully on condition that no one was arrested.
Police said the Gaullist mayor of Paris, Jean Tiberi, ordered the evacuation of the church, in the heavily immigrant Belleville district, on safety and sanitary grounds.
The government apparently wanted to avoid a repeat of last year's embarrassing occupation of a Paris church by hunger-striking African immigrants.
Their protest dragged on for two months until police wadded through a cordon of French supporters to break down the church gates with axes and forcibly eject the Africans.

Immigration is turning into the hottest issue just over a year ahead of general elections as the government and protesters accuse each other of pandering to the far-right National Front of anti-immigrant crusader Jean-Marie Le Pen.
"France is an old lady, barricaded in her home and asking for one more lock every year," said writer Pascal Bruckner.

Tens of thousands of intellectuals, artists, left-wing politicians and ordinary citizens took part in the Paris march. But the ruling RPR Gaullist party described the demonstration, and small protests in other cities as "a stinging failure".

Leaders of the protests hailed them as an awakening of public opinion which previously backed curbs on immigration. Writer Dan Franck said the various groups of protesters were now trying to agree on joint plans to keep up the momentum.
More protests are planned on Tuesday when the disputed bill goes to the National Assembly for a final reading although the government has withdrawn its most controversial clause.

The clause, intended to prevent people from developping countries from overstaying short-term visas and turning into illegal immigrants, ordered their French hosts to notify police of their departure. The government has agreed to make the foreigners responsible for reporting their own departure.
Louis Viannet, head of the Communist-led CGT trade union, said he would fight for the bill to be withdrawn altogether.

An Ipsos opinion poll suggested the French people were split and perplexed. A 59 to 34 percent majority wanted the government to maintain the bill, but people were divided evenly on the protesters' call for civil disobedience if it became law.
Fifty-four percent said they would back a movement to dispute the ideas of the National Front, to 41 percent who would either ignore or oppose it.
